citations.quote: A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: [[lem-finite-choice]] applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and the choice function of
  [[def-choice-function]] is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
([[def-topological-space]]). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
([[thm-basis-criterion]]): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
([[def-topological-space]]); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: Choose at most countable bases $\mathcal U$ for $X$ and $\mathcal V$ for $Y$ using [F1]. Their product $\mathcal U\times\mathcal V$ is at most countable by [F2], and its members $U\times V$ form a basis for $X\times Y$ by [F3]. Each such rectangle lies in $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$; every open subset of $X\times Y$ is a union of a subfamily of this countable basis, hence a countable union of those rectangles. By [F4], this proves $\mathcal B(X\times Y)\subseteq\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$.

The coordinate projections $\pi_X:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_Y:X\times Y\to Y$ are continuous by the definition of the product topology [F3]. For Borel $A\subseteq X$ and $C\subseteq Y$, $A\times C=\pi_X^{-1}(A)\cap\pi_Y^{-1}(C)$ is Borel in $X\times Y$. Thus every generator rectangle of the product sigma-algebra [F5] belongs to $\mathcal B(X\times Y)$, giving the reverse inclusion.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a bounded Borel set $W\subset\mathbb R^d$. Under
Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable
([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), so Lebesgue measure $\ell_d$ is
defined on each such set. Write $|A|:=\ell_d(A)$ for Borel $A$, and
$\mathcal B_W:=\{W\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\}$ for the trace Borel
sigma-algebra on $W$. Every member of $\mathcal B_W$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^d$
because $W$ is Borel. Define $\ell_W:\mathcal B_W\to[0,+\infty]$ by
$\ell_W(A):=\ell_d(A)$. If $(A_k)$ is pairwise disjoint in $\mathcal B_W$,
then each $A_k$ and their union are Borel in $\mathbb R^d$, so countable
additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)
=\sum_k\ell_d(A_k)=\sum_k\ell_W(A_k),$$
and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The only choice axiom used to regard $\ell_d$ as a measure in this library is
Countable Choice, as recorded in
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]].

The **finite configuration space on $W$**, denoted $\mathcal C(W)$, is the
measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by
$\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq W$.

For a finite ambient configuration $\widetilde\eta$, its observation in $W$
is $\eta=\widetilde\eta|_W$, where
$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

For a measurable rectangle $B\times C$, the map $\eta\mapsto(\eta\otimes\eta)(B\times C)=\eta(B)\eta(C)$ is measurable by [F1]. Let
$$\mathcal D:=\{A\in\mathcal B_W^{\otimes2}:\eta\mapsto(\eta\otimes\eta)(A)\text{ is measurable}\}.$$
The whole space belongs to $\mathcal D$ because its value is $\eta(W)^2$: for each integer $k\ge0$, the level set $\{\eta(W)^2\ge k\}$ is a countable union of evaluation level sets $\{\eta(W)=n\}$. The total product mass is finite. For $A\in\mathcal D$, finite additivity gives $(\eta\otimes\eta)((W\times W)\setminus A)=\eta(W)^2-(\eta\otimes\eta)(A)$; this finite-valued measurable difference is measurable by [F4], so complements belong. Countable disjoint unions belong by countable additivity, since the partial sums are measurable by [F4] and their pointwise limit is measurable by [F5]. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system containing the rectangles.

Rectangles form a pi-system and generate the product Borel sigma-algebra by [F6] and [F7]. Dynkin's theorem [F3] applied to step 1.1 therefore gives that $\eta\mapsto(\eta\otimes\eta)(A)$ is measurable for every Borel $A\subseteq W\times W$. The set $D_R$ is closed, so its product-measure evaluation is measurable.

If $\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$, then $(\eta\otimes\eta)(D_R)=\sum_{i,j=1}^n1_{\{\|x_i-x_j\|_2\le R\}}$. The $n$ terms with $i=j$ all occur since $R\ge0$; every remaining unordered pair of distinct occurrences contributes exactly two terms. Hence the displayed formula for $S_R$ is a finite nonnegative integer and is measurable by step 2.1 and [F1].

neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the

([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and

[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is

**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**

measurable. Addition $(x,\mu)\mapsto\mu+\delta_x$ is interpreted as addition

$$\mathbb E\left[\int_S h(x,\eta)\,\eta(dx)\right]=\int_S\mathbb E[h(x,\eta+\delta_x)]\,\nu(dx).$$

$$D:=\{(x,\mu)\in S\times\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S):\mu(\{x\})\ge1\}.$$

measurable. The subtraction removes one occurrence, so any other occurrences
at $x$ remain.

domain. Omit $b$ when there is no exterior condition or when the fixed

$$\mathbb E_{\theta,b}\left[\sum_{x\in\eta}h(x,\eta-\delta_x)\right]=\mathbb E_{\theta,b}\left[\int_W h(u,\eta)\lambda_\theta(u;\eta,b)\,\ell_W(du)\right].$$

additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)

([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then

For a test function $h$ as in the Statement, define on the domain where $(x,\zeta)$ contains an occurrence at $x$ $k(x,\zeta):=g(\zeta)h(x,\zeta-\delta_x),$ and set $k=0$ off that domain. The domain and deletion map are measurable by [F2]; the extensions, addition operation, and $g,h$ are measurable by [F4, F5], so $k$ is a nonnegative measurable test function for [F1]. Also the addition map is measurable by [F4], and since $g$ is finite and strictly positive, its ratio $\lambda_g(u;\eta)=g(\eta+\delta_u)/g(\eta)$ is a measurable function on $W\times\mathcal C(W)$.

finite-window Poisson probability measure on that space. For each parameter
$\theta$, let $\mathcal S_\theta\subseteq\mathcal C(W)$ be a measurable
admissible support and let $H_\theta:\mathcal S_\theta\to\mathbb R$ be
measurable. Extend the weight by zero off $\mathcal S_\theta$:
$w_\theta(\eta)=e^{-H_\theta(\eta)}$ on $\mathcal S_\theta$ and $0$
elsewhere. Put
$$Z_\theta:=\int_{\mathcal C(W)}w_\theta(\eta)\,Q(d\eta).$$
Only when $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ do these data define the finite-window Gibbs
law, with density
$$\frac{dP_\theta}{dQ}(\eta)=Z_\theta^{-1}w_\theta(\eta).$$
The support and normalizer are part of the model specification. No general
existence, mixing, consistency, or asymptotic result is included in this
definition.

Let $W$ and $\mathcal C(W)$ be as in
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]]. For $R\ge0$, put
$$D_R:=\{(x,y)\in W\times W:\|x-y\|_2\le R\}.$$
For a finite configuration $\eta$, define
$$S_R(\eta):=\frac12\big((\eta\otimes\eta)(D_R)-\eta(W)\big).$$
Here $\eta\otimes\eta$ is the product measure and the subtraction removes
the $n$ ordered self-pairs from a representation with $n=\eta(W)$ occurrences.
Thus $S_R$ counts unordered pairs of distinct occurrences at distance at most
$R$, including co-located distinct occurrences when multiplicity is present.
Then $S_R:\mathcal C(W)\to[0,\infty)$ is measurable.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a bounded Borel set $W\subset\mathbb R^d$. Under
Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable
([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), so Lebesgue measure $\ell_d$ is
defined on each such set. Write $|A|:=\ell_d(A)$ for Borel $A$, and
$\mathcal B_W:=\{W\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\}$ for the trace Borel
sigma-algebra on $W$. Every member of $\mathcal B_W$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^d$
because $W$ is Borel. Define $\ell_W:\mathcal B_W\to[0,+\infty]$ by
$\ell_W(A):=\ell_d(A)$. If $(A_k)$ is pairwise disjoint in $\mathcal B_W$,
then each $A_k$ and their union are Borel in $\mathbb R^d$, so countable
additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)
=\sum_k\ell_d(A_k)=\sum_k\ell_W(A_k),$$
and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The only choice axiom used to regard $\ell_d$ as a measure in this library is
Countable Choice, as recorded in
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]].

The **finite configuration space on $W$**, denoted $\mathcal C(W)$, is the
measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by

$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $Q$ be the unit-rate Poisson law on $\mathcal C(W)$ from
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]]. Suppose $g:\mathcal C(W)\to(0,\infty)$
is measurable, finite everywhere, and $\int g\,dQ=1$. Let $P=gQ$ and define
$$\lambda_g(u;\eta):=\frac{g(\eta+\delta_u)}{g(\eta)}.$$
Then $\lambda_g$ is a Papangelou conditional intensity for $P$ relative to
$\ell_W$ in the sense of
[[def-papangelou-conditional-intensity]].

Let $W$ and $\mathcal C(W)$ be as in
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]]. Fix an observed configuration
$\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ and a boundary convention $b$ (a specified exterior
configuration held fixed, or no exterior configuration). When a model supplies
a Papangelou conditional intensity $\lambda_\theta(u;\zeta,b)$, define its
**finite-window pseudolikelihood criterion** by
$$\operatorname{PL}_{W,b}(\theta;\eta):=\left(\prod_{x\in\eta}\lambda_\theta(x;\eta-\delta_x,b)\right)\exp\left\{-\int_W\lambda_\theta(u;\eta,b)\,\ell_W(du)\right\}.$$
The finite product counts multiplicities, the empty product is $1$, and one
occurrence is deleted in each event factor. The criterion is used only when
the displayed intensity values and integral are finite; a zero event factor
makes the criterion zero. The exterior pattern $b$ is fixed throughout the
calculation. This criterion is not asserted to be a joint likelihood, and its
definition supplies no consistency or asymptotic guarantee.

Let $W\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\mathcal C(W)$ be as in
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]], with volume $v=|W|<\infty$. For
each parameter $\theta$, let $\lambda_\theta:W\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued
Borel function and assume
$$\Lambda_\theta:=\int_W\lambda_\theta(x)\,\ell_W(dx)<\infty.$$
Extend $\lambda_\theta$ by zero off $W$ and let $P_\theta$ be the law on
$\mathcal C(W)$ of the Poisson process on $\mathbb R^d$ with intensity measure
$\nu_\theta=1_W\lambda_\theta\,d\ell_d$. Let $P_0$ be the unit-rate Poisson
law on $\mathcal C(W)$ obtained from intensity $1_W\,d\ell_d$. Then
$$\frac{dP_\theta}{dP_0}(\eta)=g_\theta(\eta):=\exp\{v-\Lambda_\theta\}\prod_{x\in\eta}\lambda_\theta(x).$$
where the product counts atom occurrences and the empty product is $1$. In
particular $P_\theta\ll P_0$. This formula explicitly chooses a common
parameter-indexed density version, so it requires no arbitrary simultaneous
selection of Radon–Nikodym representatives.

For an observed $\eta$, if every observed occurrence has positive intensity,
the log likelihood, up to the parameter-independent term $v$, is
$$\ell_\eta(\theta)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\log\lambda_\theta(x)-\Lambda_\theta.$$
If any observed occurrence has zero intensity, the likelihood is zero and its
log is $-\infty$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each

parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $\nu$ be a finite atomless Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let
$\eta$ be a Poisson point process with intensity $\nu$. Then $\eta$ is simple
almost surely: with probability one, every singleton has mass at most one.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

derivations.claim: Both $N$ and $S_R$ are finite nonnegative integer-valued measurable functions by [F2]. For $m,k\in\mathbb N_0$, the set $\{N=m,S_R=k\}$ is measurable, and on it $H_{\beta,\gamma}=-m\log\beta-k\log\gamma$ and $w=\beta^m\gamma^k$. Thus both the energy and weight are measurable by their countable measurable level-set partitions. By [F10], $e^{-H_{\beta,\gamma}(\eta)}=w(\eta)$. Since $0<\gamma\le1$, $0<w(\eta)\le\beta^{N(\eta)}$. The unit-rate reference count $N$ has law $\operatorname{Pois}(4)$ by [F9], with masses given by [F6], so $Z=\mathbb E_{P_0}w(\eta)\le\mathbb E_{P_0}\beta^N=e^{-4}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(4\beta)^n}{n!}=e^{4(\beta-1)}<\infty.$ The empty configuration contributes $P_0\{\eta=0\}=e^{-4}$ to $Z$, hence $Z\ge e^{-4}>0$. Thus [F1] defines the stated Gibbs law.

Inserting $u$ adds one point and creates exactly $T_R(u,\eta):=\eta(\{v\in W:\|v-u\|_2\le R\})$ unordered interaction pairs, counting occurrences: if the pair count is written as the number of unordered pairs, the increase is $S_R(\eta+\delta_u)-S_R(\eta)=\big(2T_R(u,\eta)+1-1\big)/2=T_R(u,\eta)$; the $1$ in the numerator is the new diagonal term removed in the definition of $S_R$. Therefore $\frac{w(\eta+\delta_u)}{w(\eta)}=\beta\gamma^{T_R(u,\eta)}.$ The same ratio holds for the normalized density because $Z$ cancels; [F3] shows that the Strauss Papangelou conditional intensity is $\lambda(u;\eta)=\beta\gamma^{T_R(u,\eta)}$.

Every singleton is a degenerate box of Lebesgue measure zero by [F7], so the unit-rate reference intensity is atomless. It is simple almost surely by [F8]. The normalized Strauss law is absolutely continuous with respect to that reference and is therefore also supported on simple configurations. Thus on a probability-one set the occurrence-pair energy is the usual simple-pattern Strauss energy.

When $\gamma=1$, $S_R$ drops out and the normalizer from the earlier calculation gives $Z=e^{4(\beta-1)}$, so the exact density is $e^{4(1-\beta)}\beta^{N(\eta)}$, matching the Poisson formula [F5]. The Papangelou intensity is the constant $\beta$, so [F4] gives pseudolikelihood $\beta^{N(\eta)}e^{-4\beta}$. The ratio of exact to pseudo likelihood is the observation-independent constant $e^4$.

Now suppose $0<\gamma<1$, let $x=(1,1)$, and compare the empty configuration $0$ with $\delta_x$. By [F1] and the fact that neither configuration has an interacting pair, their exact Gibbs density ratio is $g(\delta_x)/g(0)=\beta$. By [F4] and step 2.1, the pseudolikelihood ratio is $\frac{\operatorname{PL}(\delta_x)}{\operatorname{PL}(0)}=\beta\exp\{\beta(1-\gamma)a\},\qquad a:=|\{u\in W:\|u-x\|_2\le R\}|.$ Indeed the event factor at $x$ is $\beta$, and the integrated intensity changes from $\beta|W|$ to $\beta(|W|-(1-\gamma)a)$.

The square $[4/5,6/5]^2$ lies inside the radius-$1/2$ ball about $x$, so $a\ge4/25>0$ by [F12]. Hence $\exp\{\beta(1-\gamma)a\}>1$ by [F11], and the pseudo ratio is strictly larger than the exact ratio $\beta$. A constant multiple of the exact likelihood would have equal observation ratios, so the Strauss pseudolikelihood is not the joint likelihood in this case. The example makes no consistency or asymptotic claim.
